sections.title: What is Bit Manipulation?
sections.content:
Bit manipulation is working directly with the binary representation of integers using the CPU's native bitwise instructions. Modern CPUs perform bitwise operations in a single clock cycle, making them the fastest possible arithmetic operations - faster than division, modulo, or even multiplication.

In DSA, bit manipulation solves problems that would otherwise require extra space or multiple passes. **XOR** is the standout operator: it is its own inverse. `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a`. This lets you find missing elements, detect the unique element in an array where all others appear twice, and swap values without a temporary variable - all in O(1) space.

**Bitmasks** represent subsets of a small set (up to 30 elements) as integers. This is what makes bitmask DP viable: exponential state space (2^n subsets) stored in polynomial memory (n integers). Checking membership, adding elements, and removing elements from a subset are all single bitwise operations.

Bit manipulation appears across every DSA category - not as a standalone algorithm but as a constant-factor optimization or an O(1) trick that replaces a naive O(n) or O(log n) operation. Missing it means missing clean solutions to problems that look unrelated to binary representation on the surface.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use bit manipulation when you need to find a unique element among duplicates, check if a number is a power of 2, count set bits efficiently, represent a subset of a small set, toggle or test individual flags in a state, or compute XOR across a range. It is also the foundation for bitmask DP (covered separately). Bit tricks are not a replacement for algorithmic thinking - they are a tool to reduce constant factors and space after the algorithm is correct.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## The Six Operators

- `&` (AND) - both bits must be 1: `5 & 3 = 1` (`101 & 011 = 001`). Used to test or clear bits.
- `|` (OR) - either bit is 1: `5 | 3 = 7` (`101 | 011 = 111`). Used to set bits.
- `^` (XOR) - exactly one bit is 1: `5 ^ 3 = 6` (`101 ^ 011 = 110`). Used to toggle, find unique elements.
- `~` (NOT) - flip all bits. In two's complement: `~n = -(n + 1)`, so `~0 = -1`, `~5 = -6`.
- `<<` (left shift) - multiply by 2: `1 << k = 2^k`. Used to create bit masks.
- `>>` (right shift) - divide by 2 (arithmetic, preserves sign). `>>>` is unsigned right shift in JS.

**Key patterns**:
- `n & (n - 1)` - removes the lowest set bit from `n`. Repeating this counts all set bits.
- `n & (-n)` - isolates the lowest set bit of `n`. The core of Fenwick Tree indexing.
- `n >> k & 1` - tests whether bit `k` of `n` is set (returns 0 or 1).

## XOR Tricks

XOR properties: `a ^ a = 0`, `a ^ 0 = a`, commutative and associative. These make XOR powerful for finding hidden elements:

- **Single non-duplicate**: XOR all elements. Pairs cancel out (`a ^ a = 0`), leaving the unique element.
- **Two non-duplicates**: XOR all elements gives `x ^ y` where x and y are the two unique elements. Find any set bit in `x ^ y` (they differ there). Split all elements into two groups by that bit. XOR each group separately gives x and y.
- **XOR of range [1..n]**: follows a pattern cycling every 4: `n%4 === 0 → n`, `1 → 1`, `2 → n+1`, `3 → 0`.

## Bit Counting and Powers of 2

`n & (n - 1) === 0` means n is a power of 2 - exactly one bit is set (or n is 0; add `n > 0` check). **Brian Kernighan's algorithm** for popcount: `while (n) { count++; n &= n - 1; }` - each iteration removes one set bit, running in O(number of set bits) rather than O(bit length).

## Bitmask as Set

For a universe of `n` elements (n ≤ 30), an integer represents a subset:
- `1 << i` - set containing only element i
- `mask | (1 << i)` - add element i to mask
- `mask & ~(1 << i)` - remove element i from mask
- `mask & (1 << i)` - test if element i is in mask (non-zero if yes)
- `(1 << n) - 1` - full set of all n elements

This representation is what powers bitmask DP over subsets.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: A reference block of the most common bit manipulation patterns used across DSA problems. These are building blocks - recognizing which one applies is the skill, not memorizing the syntax.

items.name: Gray Code
items.description: A sequence where consecutive integers differ by exactly one bit. The nth Gray code is `n ^ (n >> 1)`. Converting between binary and Gray code uses XOR. Appears in problems about minimal-change sequences and circular arrangements.

items.name: Bitwise Addition Without +
items.description: Add two integers using only XOR and AND: `sum = a ^ b` gives bits without carry, `carry = (a & b) << 1` gives the carry. Repeat until carry is 0. This is how hardware adders work and appears in 'Sum of Two Integers' type problems.

items.name: Integer Square Root via Bit Shifts
items.description: Estimate square roots and bit lengths using right shifts. `Math.floor(Math.log2(n)) = 31 - Math.clz32(n)` in JS. Bit-length tricks appear in problems about representing numbers in binary and in segment tree height calculations.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(1) per operation, O(log n) for popcount in worst case
sections.explanation: All single bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, shift, NOT) are O(1) - single CPU instructions. Brian Kernighan's popcount runs in O(k) where k is the number of set bits, which is at most O(log n) for a value n. Using XOR to find a single number in an array of n elements is O(n) total (one pass), O(1) space. Bitmask operations on a 32-bit integer representing a subset of up to 30 elements are all O(1).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: JS bitwise operators coerce operands to 32-bit SIGNED integers - numbers larger than 2^31 - 1 are truncated. For n > 2^30, use `>>> 0` (unsigned right shift by 0) to treat the result as unsigned, or use `BigInt` for very large values.
`~n = -(n + 1)` in two's complement - `~0 = -1`, not `0`. Using `~` expecting a boolean-style NOT flip is a common bug; for toggling a bit, use `^ (1 << k)` instead.

Left shift overflow: `1 << 31` produces a negative number in JS (the sign bit is set). For bitmasks over 30+ elements, use `1n << BigInt(k)` with BigInt, or restructure to avoid needing more than 30 bits.
`n & (-n)` gives the lowest set bit, not the highest. Confusing these two produces wrong Fenwick Tree traversal direction (isolating highest vs lowest set bit are completely different operations).
Operator precedence: bitwise operators have lower precedence than comparison operators in JS. `n & 1 === 0` is parsed as `n & (1 === 0)` = `n & false` = 0, always. Always wrap: `(n & 1) === 0`.

items.title: Single Number
items.why: The canonical XOR trick - XOR all elements; pairs cancel to 0, leaving the unique element.

items.title: Number of 1 Bits
items.why: Tests Brian Kernighan's algorithm - repeatedly strip the lowest set bit to count set bits in O(k).

items.title: Reverse Bits
items.why: Tests extracting and placing individual bits using shift and OR - fundamental bit-level manipulation.

items.title: Sum of Two Integers
items.why: Tests bitwise addition using XOR (sum without carry) and AND+shift (carry) - requires understanding two's complement for negative numbers.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Prefix Sum is the next Others topic - a simple array technique that, like bit manipulation, is a constant companion across problems. It introduces the prefix XOR variant which directly uses bit manipulation, bridging the two topics.
